title: Oedipus at Colonus
author: Sophocles
openingText: Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, What region, say, whose city have we reached? Who will provide today with scanted dole This wanderer? 'Tis little that he craves, And less obtains—that less enough for me; For I am taught by suffering to endure, And the long years that have grown old with me, And last not least, by true nobility. My daughter, if thou seest a resting place On common ground or by some sacred grove, Stay me and set me down. Let us discover Where we have come, for strangers must inquire Of denizens, and do as they are bid.
about:
Oedipus at Colonus is the play in which the aged, blind Oedipus arrives at a sacred grove in the village of Colonus, just outside Athens, accompanied by his daughter Antigone. He has been an exile from Thebes for twenty years. He is at the end of his strength and quietly sure that the place where he is sitting is the place where he is fated to die. His other daughter Ismene arrives with news from Thebes: a new oracle has declared that whichever city holds Oedipus's body will be blessed in war, his sons are at war over the throne, and everyone wants him back. Creon comes to take him by force. Polynices comes to beg his blessing. Theseus, king of Athens, comes to give him sanctuary. The play is the day Oedipus chooses where to die.

Sophocles wrote it in his last year of life, in his nineties, and it was produced posthumously by his grandson at the City Dionysia of 401 BCE. It is in eleven scenes and is the longest of his surviving plays. Colonus was Sophocles's own birthplace; the grove he describes was the one he had walked in as a boy. The choral ode in praise of Colonus, sung in the middle of the play, was written by a man near death, in honor of his own home, while Athens was losing the Peloponnesian War.

It is unusual among the surviving Greek tragedies in that its action turns toward something like consecration. Oedipus has done nothing to redeem himself; he has simply suffered, for a very long time, and has come to understand his suffering as the work of the gods rather than his own. At the end of the play he walks into the grove on his own feet, the only mortal he allows to follow him is Theseus, and his death is not staged but reported. The earth, the messenger says, opened gently and took him in. The play is one of the most beautiful Sophocles wrote and the only one in which a tragic hero exits the world without violence.

angleCards.title: Sophocles at ninety.
angleCards.text: This is a valedictory play — written in the last year of a long life, performed after the author's death. Notice where the voice has softened from Oedipus Rex, where the anger has become something more like wonder, and what a playwright chooses to say when he knows this is the last thing he will say.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a late work — to trace how Sophocles's voice changed over a lifetime and what he chose to affirm at the end of it.

angleCards.title: Suffering as sanctity.
angleCards.text: Oedipus has done nothing to redeem himself. He has simply suffered, for a very long time. And yet the gods declare his body a blessing to whatever land receives it. The play asks whether endurance itself — without redemption, without moral transformation — can become a kind of holiness.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what the play is claiming about suffering — whether it can be sanctifying without being deserved or earned.

angleCards.title: Reconciliation, not resolution.
angleCards.text: Oedipus does not forgive his sons. He curses them. He does not make peace with the past — he pronounces on it. This is not a play about healing. Watch how the play distinguishes between resolution (which is impossible) and the stranger thing that actually happens to Oedipus at the end.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a study in what comes after tragedy when resolution is impossible — what Sophocles puts in its place.

angleCards.title: Athens and Thebes.
angleCards.text: Theseus and Creon are studies in contrast: the king who keeps his word and the man who does not, the city that offers refuge and the one that uses people. Sophocles is making an argument about political character — written, pointedly, while Athens was losing a war.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the political argument — what Sophocles is saying about Athens and Thebes, hospitality and power, and what kind of city can receive an Oedipus.

cast.name: Oedipus
cast.description: Old, blind, twenty years in exile, guided by his daughter and carrying nothing but a prophecy. His voice is quieter than it was in Oedipus Rex but the steel underneath has not softened. When Creon tries to take him by force he calls down a curse. When Polynices begs his blessing he refuses it. When Theseus offers Athens's protection he accepts. He is allowed, at the end, to walk into the grove on his own feet.

cast.name: Antigone
cast.description: Oedipus's daughter, who left Thebes to guide him into exile and has not returned in the twenty years since. She settles him on stones, fetches him water, listens to his curses without flinching. Her loyalty to him is absolute and uncomplicated. The play does not foreshadow what Sophocles wrote forty years earlier — Antigone burying her brother and dying for it — but the audience knew. Her tenderness here is sharpened by what they knew was coming.

cast.name: Ismene
cast.description: Oedipus's younger daughter, who stayed in Thebes. She arrives at Colonus on horseback, alone, the bearer of news. There is a new oracle: whichever city holds Oedipus's body will be blessed in war. His sons Eteocles and Polynices are at war over the Theban throne, and both of them want their father back not for his sake but for his bones. Ismene reports this with the tact of someone who has been carrying it for weeks.

cast.name: Theseus
cast.description: Ruler of Athens and the play's model of just kingship. He hears Oedipus out and grants him refuge with the full authority of the city — without asking him to recite his story, without holding the reception over his head. When Creon abducts the daughters Theseus rides out and brings them back. Sophocles wrote him while Athens was losing the war and on the verge of surrender; he is what the playwright's city had once been, or had imagined itself to be.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: Oedipus's brother-in-law, arrived from Thebes with armed men. He needs Oedipus — or his body — for political reasons, and he will use force when persuasion fails. He delivers a speech of soft persuasion, then has Antigone seized when Oedipus refuses, then tries to take Oedipus himself. Theseus blocks him. The Creon of this play is recognizably the Creon of Antigone — a man whose calculations are reasonable on their surface and corrupt underneath.

cast.name: Chorus of Elders
cast.description: The elders of Colonus, the small Attic village outside Athens. They are guardians of the sacred grove and frightened of Oedipus the moment they learn his name — his pollution is still real to them. Their gradual acceptance of him is the play's emotional spine. They sing the celebrated ode to Colonus halfway through, in which Sophocles, near the end of his life, wrote a song about the place he was born. They begin afraid and end mourning him.

whyItMatters.title: A Late Sophocles, Still Working
whyItMatters.body: Oedipus at Colonus was written by Sophocles in his nineties and produced posthumously by his grandson, four years after his death. It concerns an old, blind man at the end of long suffering, in the village where Sophocles himself was born, written as Athens was losing the Peloponnesian War and the city he had served all his life was in collapse. It is one of the most striking examples in literature of late style — the formal control of long practice, the tenderness of someone who has seen everything, the willingness to risk a quietness that a younger writer would not have dared. Edward Said wrote on this category and used Sophocles as one of his foundational cases.

whyItMatters.title: The Man Who Did Not Choose His Crimes
whyItMatters.body: The play returns to the question Oedipus Rex left unsettled: what is Oedipus guilty of, having done what was prophesied before he was born? In the earlier play Sophocles refused to let him off; in this one he answers more gently, but he does not contradict himself. Oedipus has not become a better man. He has simply suffered, in exile, for two decades, and Sophocles suggests that the suffering itself, undertaken without the consolation of having earned it, has reshaped him into someone the gods are willing to receive. It is not a Christian answer about penance. It is something stranger and harder: that long endurance of what was not your fault can become its own kind of standing.

whyItMatters.title: The Sacred Stranger
whyItMatters.body: Oedipus arrives in Athens as a polluted, blind, dependent stranger — the most cursed name in Greek myth, asking for shelter at the boundary of a sacred grove. The Athenians, after some hesitation, take him in. The play stages, at the end of Sophocles's life and during the collapse of his city, a different vision of what Athens is for: not the imperial power, not the conqueror, but the place where a broken man can be received and become a blessing. The earth opens and takes him in gently; only Theseus is allowed to witness it. The image of the polluted stranger who turns out to be sacred is one of the deepest in Western literature, and it runs through Christian theology, Levinas's ethics, and contemporary writing on hospitality.
